chapters.title: Partakers of the Divine Nature
chapters.teaser: Believers are said to actually share in God's own nature through his promises.
body: Verse 4 makes one of the boldest claims in the New Testament: through God's "exceeding great and precious promises," believers might become "partakers of the divine nature," having escaped the corruption that comes from worldly lust. It's language that goes further than most New Testament writers venture.

This idea became especially influential in later Christian thought, particularly in Eastern Christianity's concept of theosis, or deification — the idea that salvation means real transformation into likeness with God, not merely legal forgiveness. Here, at its earliest, it's stated almost in passing, tucked into the letter's opening argument.

chapters.title: A Ladder of Virtues
chapters.teaser: Eight qualities are chained together, each meant to build on the one before it.
body: Verses 5-7 lay out a sequence: add to faith virtue, to virtue knowledge, to knowledge temperance, to temperance patience, to patience godliness, to godliness brotherly kindness, to brotherly kindness charity. The structure — a graduated chain of linked qualities — was a familiar form in Greco-Roman moral writing, here put entirely to Christian use.

The list isn't meant as a rigid sequence to complete once and move past, but as a cumulative, "abounding" growth (v.8) — each quality reinforcing rather than replacing the last, aimed at keeping believers from being "barren nor unfruitful" in what they claim to know.

chapters.title: Forgetting Your Own Cleansing
chapters.teaser: Failing to grow spiritually is diagnosed as a kind of amnesia about one's own past.
body: Verse 9 offers an unusual diagnosis for stagnant faith: someone lacking these qualities "is blind, and cannot see afar off, and hath forgotten that he was purged from his old sins." The problem isn't framed as ignorance of doctrine but as forgetting something that already happened to them personally.

The remedy implied is memory as much as effort — recalling one's own cleansing as motivation to keep moving forward, rather than treating spiritual growth as an abstract obligation disconnected from a real, remembered starting point.

chapters.title: Eyewitness on the Mountain
chapters.teaser: Peter appeals directly to having personally witnessed Christ's glory at the Transfiguration.
body: Verses 16-18 ground the letter's authority in firsthand experience: "we have not followed cunningly devised fables... but were eyewitnesses of his majesty," recalling the voice from heaven — "This is my beloved Son" — heard "when we were with him in the holy mount," a direct reference to the Transfiguration.

The appeal matters because of what's coming in chapter 2: false teachers whose claims lack this kind of grounding. Before confronting them, the letter first establishes its own credibility on the firmest footing available — direct, personal, eyewitness testimony.

chapters.title: Not Private Interpretation
chapters.teaser: Prophecy is described as originating in the Holy Ghost, not in any individual's own will.
body: Verses 19-21 close the chapter with a foundational claim about scripture: "no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation... holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost." Prophecy's origin, in this account, lies outside human initiative entirely.

The statement functions as a hinge into chapter 2. Having established where true prophecy comes from, the letter is set up to expose false teachers whose message, by implication, comes from somewhere else entirely — their own will, not the Spirit's.

chapters.title: False Teachers Foretold
chapters.teaser: The coming crisis of false teachers is framed as a repeat of Israel's own prophetic history.
body: Verses 1-3 open by drawing a direct historical parallel: "there were false prophets also among the people, even as there shall be false teachers among you." The threat isn't presented as a new phenomenon but as the latest instance of a pattern stretching back through Israel's history.

The description that follows is severe — "damnable heresies," greed disguised in "feigned words," judgment that "lingereth not." Framing the danger as historically recurring gives the warning extra force: this isn't a hypothetical risk, it's a known pattern about to repeat itself.

chapters.title: Three Precedents for Judgment
chapters.teaser: Fallen angels, the flood, and Sodom and Gomorrah are stacked as proof God judges and rescues.
body: Verses 4-9 move rapidly through three Old Testament judgments: angels who sinned, cast into chains of darkness; "the old world," destroyed by flood except for Noah; and Sodom and Gomorrah, reduced to ashes except for Lot. Each example reinforces the same double point.

"The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment" — the three precedents aren't only warnings about judgment, they're also reassurances that rescue for the faithful has always run alongside it, even amid widespread destruction.

chapters.title: Spots and Blemishes
chapters.teaser: False teachers are described feasting within the community while quietly corrupting it from inside.
body: Verses 13-14 use unusually visceral language: these teachers are "spots... and blemishes, sporting themselves with their own deceivings while they feast with you," having "eyes full of adultery" and hearts "exercised with covetous practices." The imagery is deliberately unflattering, even repulsive.

What makes them dangerous isn't open opposition from outside but presence within — sharing meals, appearing to belong, while working corruption from the inside. The threat described isn't a rival group attacking the church; it's infiltration from people already sitting at the table.

chapters.title: Balaam's Talking Donkey
chapters.teaser: False teachers are compared to Balaam, rebuked so absurdly that even his donkey spoke sense.
body: Verses 15-16 invoke Balaam, the Old Testament prophet who "loved the wages of unrighteousness" and was famously rebuked when his own donkey spoke aloud, forbidding "the madness of the prophet." It's one of the odder Old Testament stories, deployed here as a direct comparison.

The comparison lands hard precisely because of how ridiculous the original story is — a prophet so committed to profit that God used the least likely possible messenger to correct him. False teachers driven by greed, the passage implies, are engaged in something similarly absurd, however sophisticated it may sound.

chapters.title: Worse Than Before
chapters.teaser: Two blunt proverbs close the chapter: a dog returning to vomit, a washed pig to mud.
body: Verses 20-22 end with unflinching imagery: those who briefly escape corruption only to be entangled again are "worse... than the beginning," illustrated by "the dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire."

The point isn't subtle, and it isn't meant to be. A partial, abandoned reform, in this view, leaves someone in a worse position than never having attempted change at all — not because the initial escape wasn't real, but because returning to corruption after glimpsing something better carries its own added weight.

chapters.title: Where Is the Promise?
chapters.teaser: Scoffers ask why nothing has changed since 'the fathers' died, doubting Christ will ever return.
body: Verses 3-4 name a specific objection circulating among "scoffers, walking after their own lusts": "Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation." It's one of the clearest statements in the New Testament of doubt about a delayed second coming.

The objection has an internal logic — enough time had passed by this point that the earliest generation of believers had begun dying without seeing the promised return. The letter takes the challenge seriously enough to spend the rest of the chapter answering it directly rather than dismissing it.

chapters.title: Day Like a Thousand Years
chapters.teaser: Divine timing is described as operating entirely outside ordinary human calendars and expectations.
body: Verse 8 answers the delay directly: "one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day." The point isn't a literal conversion rate but a reframing of what "delay" even means when applied to a timeless God rather than a human calendar.

What looks like an unreasonably long wait from inside human experience may not register as delay at all from outside it. The verse doesn't dissolve the tension entirely, but it relocates the problem — the promise's slowness might say more about human impatience than about God's reliability.

chapters.title: Not Slack, But Patient
chapters.teaser: The delay itself is reinterpreted as mercy — space given for repentance, not divine failure.
body: Verse 9 offers the letter's clearest answer to the scoffers: "the Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance."

What looks, from one angle, like broken timing is reframed as deliberate patience with a purpose. The wait isn't empty time before the promise catches up — it's presented as itself an expression of the same mercy the promise was about in the first place.

chapters.title: The World Undone by Fire
chapters.teaser: Cosmic dissolution by fire is described as the counterpart to the ancient world's destruction by water.
body: Verses 10-12 describe a coming judgment in dramatic terms: "the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up." The scale of the imagery matches the scale of the claim — not a local judgment, but a cosmic one.

The passage deliberately echoes the flood narrative discussed earlier in the letter, pairing water and fire as two instances of world-altering divine judgment. What follows, though, isn't just destruction — verse 13 looks past it to "new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness."

chapters.title: Calling Paul Scripture
chapters.teaser: Paul's letters are grouped among 'the other scriptures,' while frankly admitting some parts are hard to grasp.
body: Verses 15-16 reference "our beloved brother Paul," noting that his letters contain "some things hard to be understood, which they that are unlearned and unstable wrest... unto their own destruction." It's a remarkable early moment — one apostolic writing explicitly categorizing another's letters alongside "the other scriptures."

The honesty is notable too: rather than claiming Paul's writings are simple or beyond dispute, the passage admits their difficulty openly, while still treating them as authoritative enough to be misused dangerously by careless readers. The letter's very last instruction follows naturally — "grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ."
